After successfully completing the course, students can...
  • explain and apply classical theories of rhetoric in the analysis of both existing speeches and self-written speeches.
  • explain recent psychological insights into the processing of rhetorical messages, compare them with classical rhetorical insights, and apply them in the analysis of both existing speeches and self-written speeches.
  • explain and apply methods of argument analysis (Toulmin model, fact-checking, identifying fallacies), both in analyzing existing arguments and in formulating their own arguments.
  • apply classical and contemporary insights into rhetoric to write an original speech and tailor it to message, speaker, and audience.
  • deliver an original speech in a persuasive manner and reflect on their own performance.
  • reflect on their own sensitivity to, and the societal impact of, rhetorical communication.

Rhetoric, the art of persuasion, is all around us – when politicians give speeches, when influencers create content on social media, when advertisements try to persuade us, or when we ourselves want to convince someone in a conversation or a written text. In this course, we explore how these forms of persuasion work and which techniques people consciously or unconsciously use to influence others. To do that, we discuss theories of rhetoric and analyze contemporary speeches together, such as political speeches and TED Talks. What makes an argument convincing? How do emotions and speaker credibility influence the way a message is received? How can we structure and express arguments in a clear and engaging way? And how do we deliver our speeches in a persuasive manner?

In addition, we pay attention to the ethical dimension of persuasion. How do we recognize rhetorical strategies in different types of texts and conversations? When is influence legitimate, and when does it become manipulation? And how can we communicate more effectively and consciously in a variety of contexts, from academic settings to public debates and social media?

Ultimately, you will work on writing and delivering your own speech, in which you learn to use your creativity and personal viewpoints to persuade an audience.

This course is part of the learning pathway Oral Communication.

Examination:
 
The course contains a balanced mix of lectures by the lecturer and analysing or speeching by students.
  • There is a written exam (70%).
  • Every student gives a speech. Goal, context and audience are determined in consultation with the teacher. The speech is mandatory and will be graded (30%).
The use of AI is not allowed in the exam. When preparing the speech, it is permitted to use generative AI tools to develop or refine initial ideas, materials, paraphrasing, structures or outlines. In all tests, the use of AI should be transparent. Unauthorized use of AI will be reported to the examination board. Students remain responsible for (the content correctness of) their work.
